1.  Each non-black color in the input defines exactly one “geometric” object in the output.  
2.  Which object you draw depends only on **how many** input pixels of that color you have and their **relative arrangement**:  
    -  Exactly 2 input pixels, lying on the same row ⇒ straight horizontal segment.  
    -  Exactly 2 input pixels, on the same column ⇒ straight vertical segment.  
    -  Exactly 2 input pixels, neither on the same row nor column ⇒ straight diagonal segment.  
    -  Exactly 3 input pixels ⇒ “V” or inverted-“V” shape: you treat one of them as the apex and the other two as the ends of the two legs.  You draw two straight legs (on the grid: one horizontal, one vertical, or one diagonal in and one out) meeting at the apex.  The legs are drawn in the color of the two end-points; the apex cell itself keeps its original color.  
    -  4 or more input pixels ⇒ you take their minimal bounding rectangle, and you draw the **perimeter** (the four edges) of that rectangle in that color.  

Step by step how you would solve the **task input**:

1.  Identify all the nonzero colors in the input and collect the list of their coordinates.  
2.  For each color:  
    a.  Count how many pixels you have of that color and see if they lie on one row, one column, or not.  
    b.  According to the five rules above, compute exactly which new cells to fill.  
    c.  Fill those cells in that color, leaving the original pixels in place (unless overwritten by the border in the ≥4-point case, but that never happens here).

  i.e. the big box from (0,2) to (17,17).  So we draw all cells on those four edges in color 3.

• Color 6 appears exactly 3 times: at (2,3), (16,3), and (17,17).  That’s a “V” shape: the single one at row 2 is the apex and the two low ones are the ends.  Draw two straight legs: one from the apex (2,3) down to (16,3) – a vertical line in the color of that end-point (6) – and one from the apex (2,3) down-right to (17,17).  Because it’s diagonal, we march one step down and one right each time, coloring those in the color of the end-point (6).

• Color 8 appears twice at (13,10) and (16,16).  Since they are not on the same row or column, we draw a straight diagonal connecting them – coloring every cell on that grid diagonal segment in 8.  

• Colors 1 appears twice at (2,7) and (17,7) – same column (x=7).  Draw the vertical segment between them in color 1.  

When you carry that out you reproduce exactly the same combinatorial pattern of segments, V’s, and rectangles that you see in the training outputs.
